You express strong emotions at B2 level with exclamations: ¡Qué + adjective / adverb / noun!, ¡Qué + noun + tan / más + adjective!, ¡Cuánto / cuánta…!, ¡Cómo + verb!, ¡Lo + adjective + que…!, ¡Vaya + noun!, and intensifiers such as tan, tal, tanto, de un… que, and you tell exclamations apart from questions.
To build exclamations with “¡Qué…!” + adjective, adverb or noun, and with the structure “¡Qué + noun + tan / más + adjective!”.
To express quantity and intensity with “¡Cuánto / cuánta / cuántos / cuántas…!” and “¡Cómo + verb!”.
To use “¡Lo + adjective / adverb + que…!” to emphasise a quality (¡Lo bien que huele!).
To use “¡Vaya…!” and the intensifiers tan, tal, tanto, de un… que.
To write the accent correctly: qué, cuánto, cómo in exclamations, but que, cuanto, como without an accent in other functions.

Thursday, 23 April, six in the evening, El Mostrador café, Madrid. The launch starts at seven. Ecaterina has just arrived, her right hand still weak after the cast. There is already a queue in the street.
Ecaterina! How lovely to see you! And your hand? How is it?
Weak, but in one piece. But look at that queue, Lola! So many people!
They’ve been here since five. How Gil would have loved seeing this!
Faustino, what an elegant beret! Is it new?
It’s the one for special occasions. I’ve only worn it twice: at my wedding and today.
Look, the boxes have arrived. How heavy they are! Two hundred copies.
Two hundred? Wow! I don’t know if I’ll be able to sign so many with this hand.
Sign slowly. Nobody’s in a hurry. Such a queue hasn’t been seen in this street since 1980!
And smell this: fresh coffee and new books. How good the café smells today!
I’m so nervous! My legs haven’t shaken like this for forty years.
“lo que habría disfrutado” = how he would have enjoyed
Exclamations start high and fall sharply: «¡Qué BO-ni-to!» ↘. The question “¿Qué es?” rises at the end ↗. The difference is only in the melody.
In exclamations, “qué” is stressed and pronounced more strongly: ¡QUÉ alegría! As a conjunction, “que” is unstressed: Dice que viene.
The “hue” diphthong is pronounced like “ue” with a slight breath: [UE-le]. The “h” is silent.
¡Qué boina tan elegante! / ¡Qué día más largo!
What an elegant beret! / What a long day!
Exclamatory “qué” always has a written accent and the “¡” sign at the start. Without the accent (“que”) it is a conjunction or relative pronoun.
“Cuánto” agrees with the noun (cuánta gente, cuántos libros). With a verb, it is invariable: ¡Cuánto llueve!
How Gil would have enjoyed it!
You don’t know how nervous I am.
In “lo + adjective + que”, the adjective agrees with the noun, but “lo” stays neuter: lo guapA que estás, lo cansadOS que estamos.
What a day! / What a queue! (surprise, positive or negative)
Tal cola no se ha visto nunca.
Estaba tan nerviosa que no podía hablar.
Hacía un calor que no se podía respirar.
Exclamations with “¡Vaya!” can also be ironic: «¡Vaya suerte!» can mean “what luck!” or “what bad luck!”, depending on the tone.
¿Desde qué hora hay gente en la cola?
¿Cuándo se ha puesto Faustino la boina de las grandes ocasiones?
¿A qué huele el café, según Lola?
A café recién hecho y libros nuevos
Begoña Arrieta’s article for a culture blog, written on the evening of the launch. Notice the exclamations.

What a night it was yesterday on calle de las Huertas! I hadn’t seen such a queue outside a café for years: two hundred people, some since five in the afternoon, waiting for a Romanian translator in her eighties.

How silent it was when she read the chapter about 23 February! You could even hear the coffee machine. And how slowly she signed! A minute for each signature: her right hand, just out of plaster, was still shaking.

Nobody complained. Quite the opposite: people took the chance to tell her their own story. How they talked! And how she listened! It seemed that every reader left with a little of her time as well as the book.
I took lots of photos. The best one isn’t mine, but a young Romanian photographer’s. But that one, well, that one I’ll publish myself. B. A.
¿De quién es la mejor foto, según Begoña?

On 10 April, at ten in the morning, the young doctor with the rings under his eyes took Ecaterina’s cast off with an electric saw that made a dreadful noise. Rosa Elena, who had insisted on going with her, covered her ears but didn’t close her eyes. When the cast split in two, with the eight lorries cut in half, underneath appeared a pale, thin, wrinkled hand that didn’t seem to belong to anyone. Ecaterina looked at it suspiciously. “How ugly it is!” she said. The doctor replied that they all came out like that, and in two weeks it would be back to normal.

He asked her to try to make a fist. Ecaterina tried. Her fingers moved slowly, as if they had to remember how it was done. Then the doctor gave her a pen and a sheet of paper and asked her to write her name. It took Ecaterina almost a minute. The signature came out shaky, crooked, with the “E” bigger than all the rest. But it was her signature, the usual one, the one she had put on hundreds of translations. Rosa Elena clapped. So did the doctor. Ecaterina put the paper in her bag, folded in four.

The following days were for physiotherapy. The doctor had recommended she squeeze a rubber ball fifty times a day. Señor Dan, who didn’t trust rubber balls, built her a wooden device with a spring and a counter, so she could measure her progress. Rosa Elena squeezed another ball beside her, in solidarity, counting aloud in Spanish. On the fifth day, Ecaterina was already squeezing the device hard enough to jam Señor Dan’s counter. He said it was an engineering success.

She also practised her signature every evening, now with her right hand. Rosa Elena had prepared a notebook with two hundred numbered lines, one for each reader who might come to Madrid, and Ecaterina signed ten every evening after dinner. The first signatures were so shaky they looked like drawings of waves. But as the days went by, the waves grew calmer. On 20 April, Rosa Elena looked at line one hundred and ninety and said, very seriously: “How beautiful this one has come out!” Ecaterina cut it out and kept it in her purse.

On 15 April, at eleven, the doorbell rang. It was a courier with a cardboard box from Barcelona. Ecaterina looked at it for a long time before opening it. Inside, wrapped in tissue paper, were twenty copies of “La lámpara encendida”. She took one out with both hands, the good one and the weak one. It was heavier than she expected. “How beautiful it is!” she said quietly. She opened it in the middle and held it to her face. “And how good it smells!” Rosa Elena, who was beside her, smelt the book too and declared that it smelt like a new exercise book.

Ecaterina spent the whole afternoon looking at the book, without reading it. She looked at it outside, inside, from above, from below. She touched the cover with the empty drawer, the title in green letters, the flap with Andrei’s name. She read the dedication again and again. She looked for page 212 and the sentence in italics. At seven, as Andrés used to do in the bookshop, she switched on the living-room lamp, even though it was still light. Ana, who had come to see her, didn’t ask why. She already knew.

That evening she video-called Marta and showed her the book in front of the camera, turning it slowly, like someone showing off a newborn baby. Marta covered her mouth with her hands. “How wonderful! And how good Andrei’s photo looks!” she said. Andrei, who was next to her on the sofa, went red and said the photo wasn’t that special. Marta told him to be quiet. Then she asked Ecaterina to read the first sentence aloud, the one about the suitcase and the dictionary. Ecaterina read it. None of the three said anything for a while.

The twenty copies were handed out within two days. One for Ana and Mihai. One for Costel, who took it in his lorry and read it in three nights in car parks in Hungary. One for Señor Dan and his wife. One for Mrs Florica, who couldn’t read Spanish but wanted it “to show the neighbours”. One for Grandpa Gheorghe, who asked for it on the phone and promised to find someone in the village to translate it for him. And one for Rosa Elena, with a dedication written with her weak hand: “For the lorry girl. The next book is yours.”

She gave the first copy, the one she had taken out of the box with both hands, to nobody. She wrapped it in brown paper, like the bookshop’s, and put it in her suitcase. Ana asked her who it was for. Ecaterina replied that she had already promised it to someone at Christmas, and that she would give it to them in Madrid. Ana thought it must be for Marta, or for Pilar. It didn’t occur to her to think of anyone else. Ecaterina didn’t correct her.

Costel finished the book in a car park near Szeged, at four in the morning. He sent Ecaterina a message in Spanish, without a single mistake, which had taken him half an hour to write: “What a book! How I cried! And how well you write, even if you say you only know how to translate!” At the end he added that he had underlined a sentence in pen, the one on page 212, and hoped she didn’t mind. Ecaterina replied that books were made for underlining, and that Andrés underlined his too.

On 22 April they flew to Madrid. There were seven of them: Ecaterina, Ana, Mihai, Rosa Elena, Costel, who had managed to get another three days off “for cultural reasons”, and Señor Dan and his wife, who was getting on a plane for the first time since their honeymoon. Mrs Florica stayed in Bucharest, because her husband had asked her, for the first time in forty years, not to leave him alone. She sent Ecaterina a jar of zacuscă for Lola and a message: “Sign lots and don’t let your hand get tired.”

Marta and Andrei were waiting at Barajas. Andrei had longer hair, two days’ stubble and his camera hanging from Mrs Florica’s embroidered strap, already a little worn. His mother hugged him for so long that people started to stare. His father shook his hand and then, as in October, pulled him close and hugged him too. “How thin you are!” said his mother. “What a lot of hair!” said his father. Andrei told them the food in Madrid was very good, but he worked so hard he had no time to put on weight.

That night they all slept in Madrid, split between the flat on the calle del Prado, Carmen and Juan’s house in Lavapiés and a small hotel near the plaza de Santa Ana. Carmen had cooked dinner for twelve in a house built for four, as usual. Juan showed Rosa Elena how to flip the tortilla again, although she already knew how, and the little girl tossed it so high it nearly touched the ceiling light. “How this girl has grown!” said Carmen. “And what arms she has!” added Juan, who still couldn’t do it.

23 April dawned sunny. It was World Book Day, and in the streets of the centre there were booksellers’ stalls and flower stands. Inés Vidal arrived from Barcelona on the first morning train, with a red rose in her hand. She explained to Ecaterina that in Catalonia, on that day, people gave each other roses and books, and that she had brought the rose because Ecaterina had already written the book. Ecaterina smelt it and told her nobody had given her a rose since 1986. Inés asked her who the last one had been. Ecaterina smiled and didn’t answer.

In the morning, Ecaterina and Marta walked among the World Book Day stalls on calle de las Huertas and in the plaza de Santa Ana. At one of them, among newly published novels, they saw “La lámpara encendida”. It was the first time Ecaterina had seen her book on sale, in a place where anyone could buy it without knowing her. She stood still in front of the stall. The bookseller, a young man with glasses, asked whether she would like a recommendation. Ecaterina said yes. The young man talked to her about the book for five minutes without knowing who she was. Marta had to walk away so as not to laugh.

In the afternoon, at five, the queue began to form outside El Mostrador. By six it reached the corner. By half past six it went round the block. Lola had put all the café’s chairs inside, and all the ones from Faustino’s stall, and even so there wasn’t room for half the people. There were readers of all ages: students with backpacks, ladies with the book already bought under their arms, elderly couples, a group of Romanians from Madrid with a small flag. And in the front row, reserved with a sign, an empty chair beside the lamp.

Pilar had arrived from Seville on the three o’clock high-speed train, with a bunch of orange blossom wrapped in newspaper. She gave it to Ecaterina at the door and told her it came from the orange trees in the hospital courtyard, cut that very morning. The whole café smelt of orange blossom and coffee. Carmen and Juan were sitting in the second row, next to the twins from Lavapiés, who were arguing about whether orange blossom smelt better than roses. Begoña and Lucas had stayed standing by the door, cameras round their necks, like two bodyguards.

Ecaterina arrived at six, on Marta’s arm. Lola came out to meet her at the door and hugged her very carefully, because of her hand. Faustino was sitting at the table at the back, in a new beret of dark blue velvet, which according to him was the one for special occasions. Ecaterina told him what an elegant beret it was. Faustino replied that he had only worn it twice: at his wedding and that day. The boxes with the two hundred copies for sale were stacked behind the bar. Lola said how heavy they were. Ecaterina said she wished they were heavier.

At seven o’clock sharp, Lola switched off all the lights in the café except one: the lamp at the back. There was total silence. Inés spoke first, briefly, about how the manuscript had reached her inbox one Christmas night, with three lines and a last-minute correction. Then Ecaterina sat down by the lamp, opened the book with her left hand and read the chapter about 23 February 1981. She read slowly, in her usual firm voice. For twenty minutes nothing could be heard but her voice and, now and then, Lola’s coffee machine, which nobody dared switch off.

When she finished, nobody clapped for a few seconds. Then everyone clapped at once, on their feet, including those outside in the street, who had only been able to listen through the open door. Marta then sat down beside Ecaterina and read the last page, the one Inés had forbidden her to touch. Ecaterina listened with her eyes closed, the way Andrés used to listen to Rayuela. When Marta reached the last sentence, her voice broke. Ecaterina took her hand with her weak hand, and Marta finished reading.

Then the signing began. Ecaterina refused to use the stamp Inés had brought just in case. She signed with her right hand, slowly, one book after another. Each signature took her almost a minute, and by the tenth her wrist hurt. But nobody was in a hurry. Each reader used that minute to tell her something: a letter they never sent, a bookshop that no longer existed, a love from another country. Ecaterina listened to them all. She told Ana afterwards that she had heard two hundred stories that night, and that each one could have been a book.

There was a bit of everything in that queue. An eighty-year-old gentleman brought her a photo of La Lámpara in 1972, with a young woman in the doorway who wasn’t Ecaterina but Andrés’s wife, Pilar’s mother. Pilar saw it and burst into tears, because she had no photo of her mother in the bookshop. The gentleman gave it to her. A translation student asked her to sign her book “for a future translator who is afraid”. Ecaterina wrote: “Fear can be translated too. And it passes.” A Romanian couple asked her to sign in Romanian, and she did, her hand shaking with laughter.

Andrei took photos all night. Begoña, who had come with Lucas and stayed standing by the door, had reminded him of her request: she wanted a photo of Ecaterina signing, with her good hand. Andrei got it at a quarter past nine. It showed Ecaterina bent over a book, with Andrés’s tortoiseshell glasses on the tip of her nose, the lamp behind her, and in front of her a very old lady crying as she told her something. Begoña looked at it on the camera screen and said nothing. That night, on her blog, she wrote a report that ended by saying she would publish that photo herself.

At eleven, the books ran out. All two hundred. Lola had to write down the names of forty people who had been left without a copy, to send them signed ones later. Costel had spent the evening behind the bar helping Lola, serving coffee and explaining to anyone who would listen that he had brought the first hundred books by lorry from Bucharest. Rosa Elena had fallen asleep on a chair, with Inés’s rose in her hand. Señor Dan had counted the signatures: two hundred and fourteen, including the books people had brought from home.

When the last reader had left, Ecaterina opened the small suitcase she had brought and took out the parcel wrapped in brown paper. She unwrapped it slowly. It was the first copy, the one she had taken out of the box with both hands. She opened it at the first page and wrote under the printed dedication, with her right hand, trembling, a single line: “At last, delivered. E.” Then she got up, went to the shelf at the back, the one just under the lamp, where the counter used to be, and placed it there, standing up, with the cover facing the room.

Lola came over and asked whether she wanted her to sell it. Ecaterina said no. That book was not for selling or lending. It was for Andrés, she had promised it to him at Christmas, and that was the only place she could give it to him. Lola nodded, without saying anything, and wrote in the customers’ notebook, on the first page, below the note to the translator who came back: “This book is not lent. It belongs to the bookseller.” Marta, who had seen it all from the doorway, had to step outside for a moment.

Before she left, Begoña came up to Ecaterina for the first time all evening. She shook her hand, very seriously, and told her she had photographed many wars and very few book launches, but this had been the only one where nobody looked at their watch. Ecaterina thanked her for the cover photo, for the call to the art director, for hiring Andrei. Begoña replied: “Don’t thank me. That boy has a good eye. And you write well. The rest is luck.” Then she put on her sunglasses, although it was night, and left.

It was almost midnight when they all came out into calle de las Huertas. The bronze plaque shone under the green light in the window. Inside, at the back, the lamp was still on, and below it, the book. Ecaterina leaned on Ana’s arm and stood looking at the café for a moment. Her hand hurt, her legs hurt, her face hurt from smiling. “What a day!” she said. “So many people! And so many stories!” Then she added, more quietly, almost to herself: “How he would have laughed to see me signing with this handwriting!”

In the taxi back, Rosa Elena woke for a moment and asked Ecaterina whether there would be so many people the next day too. Ecaterina explained that the next day they were going to Seville, for another launch, in a small bookshop in a district called Triana, where the streets smelt of orange trees. Rosa Elena asked whether there was a lamp there too. Ecaterina said she didn’t know, but Pilar had promised her a courtyard with orange trees. Rosa Elena said then she would take her camera. And she went back to sleep, with Inés’s rose still in her hand.
